newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil starts paying price for CVRD auction delay.
newsitem.headline: Brazil starts paying price for CVRD auction delay.

text.p: Brazil will start losing money from May 5 because of the delay in the privatisation sale of mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD), the head of the National Development Bank (BNDES) said in a newspaper interview Sunday.
Latin America's largest privatisation so far had originally been set for April 29, but has been rescheduled repeatedly due to a flood of court injunctions.

Had the sale been allowed to go ahead as originally planned, the National Treasury would have received Monday at least $2.8 billion expected to be raised by the auction, BNDES president Luiz Carlos Mendonca de Barros told local Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper.
"From Monday, the Treasury starts to suffer a real loss because the auction has not taken place," Mendonca de Barros said.

"If the sale had taken place on April 29...the Treasury would have had at least three billion reais ($2.8 billion) in its coffers and these funds would have been used to reduce debt...From Monday, the country is losing money," he said.
The BNDES is examining whether there is a case to lodge its own lawsuit because of losses suffered by the delay, he added.
The bank has said it is ready to hold the sale on Monday, but a high court judge who is considering a government appeal against the lawsuits has already said his decision may not come until Tuesday.

In the Folha interview, Mendonca de Barros said the sale would take place this week as long as the legal problems were resolved but he did not want to say exactly when he thought it was likely to happen.
Seen as the key test to President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's commitment to state reform, the sale of CVRD has raised considerable opposition from nationalists and leftists.
Opponents have accused the government of selling for a pittance the country's mineral wealth such as the Carajas iron ore mine, which contains the biggest iron ore deposit in the world.

Two groups have registered to bid for the maximum 45 percent voting stake, one led by local steel firm CSN and another headed by Brazil's largest private industrial conglomerate Grupo Votorantim and South Africa's Anglo-American Corp.
While the Votorantim and Anglo-American consortium is already well-defined, the CSN-led group is continuing to negotiate with a number of companies.
Local Jornal do Brasil newspaper said Sunday that the U.S. Citibank was the latest new member after deciding to contribute to othe ffshore investment fund Opportunity Asset Management.
CSN officials could not immediately be reached to confirm the report.

In addition to Opportunity, the CSN-led consortium contains four local pension funds and NationsBank Corp, while South African mining company Gencor has signed a letter of intent to join, should the group win the auction. ((-- Caroline Bulloch, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151))
